title: Software Development — Lectures 02–10 Review
description: 269 slide-based practice questions covering tools and Git, software quality, collaborative development, JUnit and unit testing, TDD, broader software testing, debugging, and common coding mistakes.
context: This bank was built from the CSCI 2134 lecture decks for Lectures 02–10. The older course midterms were used as a question-style model; the lecture slides remain the source of the review content.

The bank includes single-best-answer, Roman-numeral combination, ordered-workflow, scenario/application, code/JUnit interpretation, and select-all-that-apply questions. Explanations include the lecture/slide source range for review.

questions.question: Which statement best matches the lecture's reason for using software-development tools?
options: Only the implementation phase is too complex to do manually.
Different phases of software development create different needs that specialized tools can support.
Tools are mainly useful for large teams, not individual developers.
A single compiler can replace most other software-development tools.
questions.explanation: The lecture places tools across the full development cycle, not just implementation. Source: Lecture 02, slides 4-6.

questions.question:
Which of the following was listed as a testing framework rather than a build tool or version-control 
system?
options: JUnit
Maven
Git
gcc <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 5 / 65>
questions.explanation: JUnit is the testing-framework example; Maven is a build tool, Git version control, and gcc a compiler. Source: Lecture 02, slides 6.

questions.question: Which IDE capability is described as typically invoking an external tool such as Git or SVN?
options: Refactoring
Version control
Editing
Profiling
questions.explanation: The IDE may integrate version control by invoking external systems such as Git or SVN. Source: Lecture 02, slides 7.

questions.question:
Which of the following IDE features are listed in the lecture?
I. On-the-fly error detection
II. Complex find and replace
III. Integrated debugging
IV. Automatic proof that the program is correct
V. Links to documentation
options: I, II, III, and V
I, III, and IV
II, IV, and V
I, II, III, IV, and V
questions.explanation: The lecture lists I, II, III, and V; it does not claim an IDE proves program correctness. Source: Lecture 02, slides 7-8.

questions.question: What is the main trade-off the lecture identifies for modern IDEs?
options: They are easy to learn but slow to use.
They have substantial functionality and can improve productivity, but can be hard to learn.
They eliminate the need for command-line tools.
They are useful only when the course requires IntelliJ.
questions.explanation: IDEs are complex because of their many menus/features, but that capability supports productivity. Source: Lecture 02, slides 9.

questions.question: For most compiled languages, what is the role of a linker in the diagram shown in lecture?
options: It converts source files directly into comments.
It combines compiled object files into an executable.
It formats source code consistently.
It stores old program versions.
questions.explanation: The slide shows multiple source files compiled to object files and then linked into an executable. Source: Lecture 02, slides 10.

questions.question: Why is simply making copied folders a poor long-term version-control strategy?
options: Copied folders cannot contain source code.
It becomes difficult to name, locate, back up, compare, and coordinate many copies as projects and teams grow.
Operating systems prohibit multiple copies of the same program.
Copies cannot be shared between developers.
questions.explanation: The lecture emphasizes consistency, location/backup, tracking changes, and collaboration problems with copying. Source: Lecture 02, slides 11-12.

questions.question: The lecture compares a version-control system to a bank primarily because both systems:
options: Require all work to occur on one computer.
Track transactions/changes, support multiple users, and make it possible to revisit earlier states.
Store only the most recent state.
Prevent people from working concurrently.
questions.explanation: The bank analogy highlights deposits/withdrawals, transaction tracking, multiple users, and reversibility. Source: Lecture 02, slides 13.

questions.question: Which description of a repository is correct according to the lecture?
options: A repository is only a remote server.
A repository is a collection of files that make up a software project and may be local or remote.
A repository is only a folder containing compiled executables.
A repository is the same thing as a single branch.
questions.explanation: The lecture defines a repository broadly and explicitly says it may be local or remote. Source: Lecture 02, slides 14.

questions.question:
Why can a version-control system efficiently preserve many versions without storing a complete 
duplicate for every version?
options: It stores only comments, never code.
It can store differences between consecutive versions and reconstruct versions as needed.
It deletes all but the newest version.
It compresses every project into a single source file.
questions.explanation: The slide notes that systems may store diffs between consecutive versions and regenerate versions when required. Source: Lecture 02, slides 15.

questions.question:
A developer begins work on an existing project. Which sequence best matches the workflow presented 
in the lecture?
options: Push modify pull commit → → →
Pull modify commit push → → →
Commit clone push modify → → →
Modify push pull commit → → →
questions.explanation: For existing work, update the working copy, modify, commit locally, then push shared commits. Source: Lecture 02, slides 16-17.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes commit, push, and pull?
options: Commit sends changes to the remote; push creates a local checkpoint; pull deletes local changes.
Commit records a local repository version; push uploads commits to a remote; pull downloads remote changes into the working copy/repository.
All three commands do the same thing at different speeds.
Pull is used only when creating a new repository.
questions.explanation: That is the command-role distinction presented on the jargon/workflow slides. Source: Lecture 02, slides 17.

questions.question:
Which item should normally be excluded from a source repository when it can be regenerated from 
source?
options: Source code
Documentation
Test data
Compiled object/class files and executables
questions.explanation: The repository should keep originating/non-regenerable artifacts and omit regenerable compiled artifacts. Source: Lecture 02, slides 18.

questions.question: Why does branching reduce the risk of experimental feature work?
options: A branch deletes the main branch until the feature is complete.
A branch provides an independent development line so changes can be made without immediately affecting main.
Only one developer can use a branch.
Branches prevent merges.
questions.explanation: The branch is a duplicate/independent code base from the current repository and can later be merged. Source: Lecture 02, slides 19-21.

questions.question: Which practice does the lecture recommend when starting a new feature?
options: Make a fresh branch, develop there, then merge back when finished and tested.
Edit the main branch directly and make one commit at the end. <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 7 / 65>
Download a ZIP copy from the Git web interface.
Create a separate remote repository for every file.
questions.explanation: The branch-development-merge pattern is the stated best practice. Source: Lecture 02, slides 21.

questions.question:
Two developers need to modify the same source file. Which approach is described as more efficient but 
requiring conflict handling?
options: Lock the file so only one developer can edit it.
Let both developers modify their copies and merge later.
Email alternate lines of the file to each other.
Prevent both developers from committing.
questions.explanation: The 'multiple access, merge later' approach improves parallel efficiency but may require merge/conflict resolution. Source: Lecture 02, slides 22.

questions.question: Which statement about Git matches the lecture?
options: Git requires centralized locking before any file can be edited.
Git keeps a local copy of the repository and supports multiple developers working on the same file.
Git is intended only for single-developer projects.
Git cannot represent multiple branches.
questions.explanation: Those are explicit properties listed for Git. Source: Lecture 02, slides 23.

questions.question: In the lecture's Git mental model, what is 'origin'?
options: The first commit hash
The primary local branch
The primary remote repository
The current working directory
questions.explanation: The slide identifies master/main as the primary branch and origin as the primary remote repository. Source: Lecture 02, slides 25.

questions.question: What does a Git commit hash primarily provide?
options: A human-readable branch description
A unique identifier for a particular commit/version
A password for the remote repository
The number of files in the commit
questions.explanation: The Git mental-model slide describes each commit/version as having a hash identifier. Source: Lecture 02, slides 25.

questions.question:
Which action is appropriate when starting from an existing remote repository rather than creating a 
brand-new repository?
options: git clone the remote repository
git init and ignore the remote
git reset --hard before any files exist
git rm the project directory
questions.explanation: The lecture distinguishes initialization of a new project from cloning an existing repository. Source: Lecture 02, slides 26-27.

questions.question:
After creating a feature branch with `git branch feature-x`, what command moves the working state 
onto that branch in the lecture?
options: git status feature-x
git checkout feature-x
git push feature-x
git log feature-x
questions.explanation: `checkout` switches to the specified branch/commit. Source: Lecture 02, slides 28-29.

questions.question: Which sequence correctly describes Git's local two-step commit process for a modified file?
options: commit the file, then stage it
stage/add the file, then commit the staged files
push the file, then commit it
checkout the file, then pull it
questions.explanation: Files are first staged with `git add`, then the staged set is committed. Source: Lecture 02, slides 30.

questions.question:
A feature branch is complete and tested. Which sequence best matches the lecture's completion 
workflow?
options: On main: merge the feature branch, then push main to the remote.
Delete main, rename the feature branch, and avoid pushing.
Push the feature branch, reset main to an old commit, then pull.
Re-clone the project and copy the feature files into main.
questions.explanation: The lecture merges the branch into main and then pushes the updated main branch. Source: Lecture 02, slides 31-33.

questions.question: Which Git command is most directly used to inspect how two versions/files differ?
options: git diff
git status
git branch
git push
questions.explanation: The difference slide uses `git diff` to compare versions. Source: Lecture 02, slides 34-36.

questions.question: Which pairing is correct?
options: git log — show commit history; git status — show current branch and file state
git log — upload changes; git status — merge branches
git log — remove a file; git status — undo a commit
git log — create a branch; git status — clone a repository
questions.explanation: Those are the roles presented for log and status. Source: Lecture 02, slides 34-36.

questions.question:
Select all that apply. Which statements are consistent with the lecture's treatment of removing/undoing 
changes?
options: `git rm` removes a tracked file from the repository history going forward.
`git revert` creates a new commit that undoes a specified commit without discarding later history.
`git reset --hard` can discard succeeding commits and should be used cautiously.
`git push` is the recommended way to undo a local commit.
questions.explanation: The first three match the removal/revert/reset slides; push is not an undo command. Source: Lecture 02, slides 37-38.

questions.question: Which behavior is explicitly recommended as a Git best practice in the lecture?
options: Download the code from the Git web interface whenever you want a fresh copy.
Edit source directly in the Git web interface for convenience.
Use `git status` often to confirm your branch and what will be committed.
Avoid branches so the history remains linear.
questions.explanation: Frequent `git status` checks are explicitly recommended; the other options contradict the best-practices slides. Source: Lecture 02, slides 39-42.

questions.question:
A developer is about to begin a risky feature. Which plan best matches the lecture's overall Git 
guidance?
options: Make a feature branch, commit coherent checkpoints as work progresses, verify status, merge when tested, and push the result.
Make a folder copy, work for a week without commits, then replace the remote repository.
Work directly on main, never pull, and use the web editor to fix conflicts. <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 9 / 65>
Create one commit per project regardless of project length.
questions.explanation: This combines the lecture's branch, commit, status, merge, and push guidance. Source: Lecture 02, slides 39-42.

questions.question:
Why does the lecture question whether first-year quality criteria are sufficient for large software 
systems?
options: Large systems do not need to function correctly.
Functionality, algorithm appropriateness, and basic formatting/commenting are useful but do not capture all the quality concerns of large, maintained systems.
Large systems cannot be tested.
Formatting is the only relevant quality criterion in large systems.
questions.explanation: The lecture uses the first-year criteria as a starting point and then expands to broader external and internal quality characteristics. Source: Lecture 03, slides 4.

questions.question: Which pairing correctly reflects the two software-quality perspectives introduced in the lecture?
options: User perspective = internal implementation; developer perspective = external functionality
User perspective = external functionality; developer perspective = internal implementation
User perspective = maintainability only; developer perspective = usability only
Both perspectives consider exactly the same criteria <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 11 / 65>
questions.explanation: The slide explicitly labels user quality as external/functionality and developer quality as internal/implementation. Source: Lecture 03, slides 5.

questions.question:
Which user-perspective quality criterion concerns continuing to function despite invalid inputs or 
stressful environmental conditions?
options: Robustness
Integrity
Accuracy
Adaptability
questions.explanation: Robustness is defined as functioning in the presence of invalid inputs or stressful conditions. Source: Lecture 03, slides 6.

questions.question:
Which user-perspective criterion is most directly about preventing unauthorized or improper access to 
programs and data?
options: Reliability
Integrity
Usability
Efficiency
questions.explanation: Integrity is the access-protection criterion on the slide. Source: Lecture 03, slides 6.

questions.question:
A system produces quantitatively correct results but consumes excessive memory and execution time. 
Which user-perspective criterion is most clearly poor?
options: Efficiency
Accuracy
Reliability
Usability
questions.explanation: Efficiency concerns minimal use of system resources such as memory and execution time. Source: Lecture 03, slides 6.

questions.question:
Which developer-perspective criterion is the ease with which a software system can be modified to add
capabilities, improve performance, or correct defects?
options: Maintainability
Portability
Reusability
Testability
questions.explanation: That is the lecture's definition of maintainability. <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 59 / 65> Source: Lecture 03, slides 7.

questions.question:
Which developer-perspective criterion focuses on understanding the entire system at both 
organizational and detailed-statement levels?
options: Readability
Understandability
Flexibility
Portability
questions.explanation: Understandability extends comprehension to both system organization and detailed statements. Source: Lecture 03, slides 7.

questions.question: What caution does the lecture give about software-quality characteristics?
options: All characteristics can always be maximized simultaneously.
Only user-perspective characteristics matter.
You may not be able to achieve all characteristics, and some can oppose one another.
Developer-perspective characteristics are independent of design.
questions.explanation: The slide explicitly warns that not all characteristics can necessarily be achieved together. Source: Lecture 03, slides 8.

questions.question: What is the General Principle of Software Quality as stated in the lecture?
options: The highest-quality software is always the largest software.
Improving software quality reduces development costs.
Quality matters only after release.
Quality can be measured only by users.
questions.explanation: The lecture explicitly names this cost relationship the General Principle of Software Quality. Source: Lecture 03, slides 9.

questions.question: Why does the lecture call software a liability?
options: Software never changes once deployed.
All software needs maintenance as APIs, standards, user needs, and defects change; more software therefore creates more maintenance cost.
Software cannot be reused.
Only hardware creates maintenance costs.
questions.explanation: The slide lists software rot, obsolescence, and defects as ongoing maintenance liabilities. Source: Lecture 03, slides 10.

questions.question: According to the lecture, what is a good size for a software project?
options: As large as possible
Exactly 10,000 lines
As small as possible while meeting the need
The size is irrelevant to maintenance cost
questions.explanation: The lecture's answer is 'as small as possible' because more software means more maintenance. Source: Lecture 03, slides 10.

questions.question:
Which action does the lecture identify as the minimum a new programmer should reliably do on a 
project?
options: Rewrite the architecture
Produce readable code
Replace the test suite
Commit broken code to reveal problems early
questions.explanation: The slide contrasts the worst action, committing broken code, with the least you should do: produce readable code. Source: Lecture 03, slides 11-12.

questions.question: Select all that apply. Which characteristics are associated with readable code in the lecture?
options: Divided into small logical units
Documented logically
Consistently formatted using a common standard
Maximally coupled to other classes
Easy to comprehend
questions.explanation: Readable code is easy to comprehend, logically organized, documented, and consistently formatted; high coupling is undesirable. Source: Lecture 03, slides 12.

questions.question: What does the lecture mean by testable code?
options: Code that never needs any tests
Code whose units/components/system can be tested and verified for defects
Code that uses no methods
Code that compiles without warnings
questions.explanation: Testability is framed as being able to test units, components, and the system. Source: Lecture 03, slides 13.

questions.question: Which combination best describes highly understandable code according to the lecture?
options: Readable, logically structured at a high level, low coupling, high cohesion
Readable, high coupling, low cohesion, no interfaces
Short, undocumented, and platform-specific
Only well formatted; design is irrelevant <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 13 / 65>
questions.explanation: The lecture explicitly connects understandability with readability, high-level structure, low coupling, and high cohesion. Source: Lecture 03, slides 14-18.

questions.question: What is coupling?
options: The degree to which methods within a class support a single purpose
The density of dependencies among classes
The number of tests in a suite
The amount of documentation in a source file
questions.explanation: Coupling is defined as the density of dependencies among classes. Source: Lecture 03, slides 15.

questions.question: Why is low coupling preferred?
options: It guarantees zero defects.
Changes to one class are less likely to force changes in many other classes.
It eliminates the need for interfaces.
It makes every class larger.
questions.explanation: High coupling spreads change through dependent classes; low coupling limits that effect. Source: Lecture 03, slides 15.

questions.question: What is the central idea of cohesion in the lecture?
options: Each class should represent a single concept and its methods should be directly applicable to that concept.
Every class should contain as many unrelated responsibilities as possible.
Cohesion measures the number of classes in a package.
High cohesion means many dependencies between classes.
questions.explanation: The lecture defines cohesion around a focused class purpose and methods that belong to that purpose. Source: Lecture 03, slides 16-17.

questions.question:
A small feature change requires edits to many unrelated parts of the system. What does the lecture 
suggest this indicates?
options: Excellent maintainability
Poor maintainability
High portability
High usability
questions.explanation: Maintainable code should permit small changes without widespread modifications. Source: Lecture 03, slides 19-20.

questions.question:
Which characteristics support highly maintainable code according to the lecture?
I. Readability
II. Testability
III. Logical high-level structure
IV. Understandability
V. Deliberately high coupling
options: I, II, III, and IV
I, III, and V
II and V
I, II, III, IV, and V
questions.explanation: The lecture lists I-IV as supports for maintainability; high coupling works against it. Source: Lecture 03, slides 19-20.

questions.question: Which characteristic is most important for reusable code according to the lecture?
options: A well-defined interface with general-purpose functionality
Dependence on many project-specific classes
No specification of what the code does
Using as many nonstandard libraries as possible
questions.explanation: Reusable code needs a well-defined interface, general-purpose functionality, and specification by behavior rather than implementation. Source: Lecture 03, slides 21.

questions.question:
How does the lecture distinguish flexibility from maintainability?
<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 14 / 65>
options: Flexibility concerns easy large adaptation to new purposes/environments, while maintainability focuses on smaller changes and fixes.
Flexibility is a user-perspective criterion; maintainability is not.
Maintainability requires high coupling; flexibility requires low coupling.
There is no distinction.
questions.explanation: The lecture frames flexibility as adaptation/extension for new uses, while maintainability is ease of making smaller changes. Source: Lecture 03, slides 22.

questions.question: Which design choice best supports portability in the lecture?
options: Hard-code platform-specific dependencies throughout the application.
Encapsulate platform dependencies and avoid unnecessary nonstandard libraries.
Use only undocumented libraries.
Rewrite every standard-library function yourself.
questions.explanation: Portable code encapsulates platform dependencies and avoids unnecessary nonstandard libraries. Source: Lecture 03, slides 23-24.

questions.question: When should a developer consider implementing functionality instead of using an available library?
options: Always, because libraries reduce readability
When no suitable third-party/standard functionality exists or the available option does not meet the need
Whenever a library is standard
Only when the program has no tests
questions.explanation: The slide recommends first finding third-party/standard functionality, then writing your own only when necessary. Source: Lecture 03, slides 24.

questions.question:
According to the key takeaways, where can a newer developer have the biggest immediate impact on 
software quality?
options: Readability and testability
Vendor selection and marketing
Hardware design and networking
Only user-interface aesthetics
questions.explanation: The key-takeaway slide explicitly identifies readability and testability as the biggest areas of impact for new developers. Source: Lecture 03, slides 25.

questions.question: Which three factors does the lecture identify as primary contributors to readability?
options: Logical structure, documentation, and consistent formatting/layout/style
Execution speed, memory usage, and file size
Number of classes, number of comments, and number of tests
Compiler choice, operating system, and network speed
questions.explanation: Those three areas are the lecture's organizing framework for readable code. Source: Lecture 04, slides 4.

questions.question: Which statement best matches the lecture's guidance on method size?
options: Every method must contain exactly one statement.
Methods should normally fit on one screen, and large public methods can often call smaller private methods.
Large methods are more readable because all logic is in one place.
Only private methods may be decomposed.
questions.explanation: The slide advocates small logical units and decomposition of large public methods/code blocks. Source: Lecture 04, slides 5.

questions.question:
What does the lecture say about Java source files and public classes?
<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 16 / 65>
options: A file should contain no more than one public class.
A file must contain at least five public classes.
Public classes should never be placed in files.
All nested classes must be public.
questions.explanation: The slide explicitly notes no more than one public class per file. Source: Lecture 04, slides 5.

questions.question: A method contains a deeply nested 80-line block. Which refactoring direction best matches the lecture?
options: Add more nesting so the control structure is explicit.
Move coherent portions into smaller private methods to reduce block size and nesting.
Remove all method calls.
Duplicate the block in another class.
questions.explanation: Large/nested blocks can often be transformed into smaller units that call private methods. Source: Lecture 04, slides 5.

questions.question: Select all that apply. Which information belongs in documentation when relevant?
options: Purpose of the code
Assumptions not obvious from the code
Authorship and origin/citations
Reasons for what the code is doing
A comment restating every assignment statement
questions.explanation: The lecture emphasizes purpose, assumptions, reasoning, authorship, and sources; narration of obvious statements is discouraged. Source: Lecture 04, slides 6-7.

questions.question: Which information is specifically expected for class-method documentation?
options: Only the author's name
Purpose/description, method-specific assumptions, parameters and parameter assumptions, and return information
Only the number of lines in the method
The complete Git history
questions.explanation: The documentation table lists those items for class methods. Source: Lecture 04, slides 7.

questions.question:
Why is a comment such as `// declare integer variable` beside `int size;` considered poor 
documentation?
options: Comments are never allowed beside variables.
It merely restates what the code already says and adds clutter rather than useful intent.
Integer variables cannot be commented.
Comments must contain URLs.
questions.explanation: The lecture's rule is that comments that simply restate the code are unnecessary and reduce readability. Source: Lecture 04, slides 8.

questions.question: Which principle about layout/style is emphasized most strongly?
options: One brace style is objectively correct for all organizations.
Consistency with the team's chosen style matters more than personal preference.
Layout has no connection to program structure.
Developers should change style from file to file to show authorship.
questions.explanation: The lecture says good style can be subjective, while consistent representation of logical structure is the objective goal. Source: Lecture 04, slides 9-10.

questions.question:
Which are objectives of layout and style?
I. Accurately represent logical structure
II. Consistently represent logical structure
III. Improve readability
<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 17 / 65>

IV. Make modifications easier to make and match
V. Make every file visually unique
options: I, II, III, and IV
I, III, and V
II and V
I, II, III, IV, and V
questions.explanation: I-IV are stated objectives; V conflicts with consistency. Source: Lecture 04, slides 10.

questions.question: Which change would most directly improve the poorly formatted code examples in the lecture?
options: Remove all whitespace
Use consistent indentation and spacing so the nesting and logical blocks are visually apparent
Move all code onto one line
Replace meaningful names with one-letter names
questions.explanation: The sequence of slides progressively adds indentation/layout to reveal code structure. Source: Lecture 04, slides 11-14.

questions.question: Why should tabs and spaces not be mixed for indentation?
options: Because Java forbids spaces
Because mixed indentation can render differently and make structure inconsistent or misleading
Because tabs disable comments
Because spaces prevent compilation
questions.explanation: The lecture explicitly warns not to mix spaces and tabs when indenting. Source: Lecture 04, slides 13.

questions.question: What is the purpose of blank lines in readable source code?
options: To increase the source-file line count
To separate blocks of functionality such as declarations, decisions, loops, and other logical sections
To replace indentation
To mark compile errors
questions.explanation: The blank-lines slide treats whitespace as a visual separator between logical blocks. Source: Lecture 04, slides 15.

questions.question: Which item belongs in the identifying block at the top of a source file?
options: Purpose/description of the file or code
A copy of every test result
The current CPU temperature
All previous versions of the file
questions.explanation: The lecture lists authorship, purpose, description, and other identifying information for the file header. Source: Lecture 04, slides 17.

questions.question: What should comments inside code primarily describe?
options: The code's purpose and the reason for complex or non-obvious parts
Every semicolon and brace
Only the variable types
Nothing; internal comments are always bad
questions.explanation: Comments should explain purpose/reasoning and be close to the code they describe. Source: Lecture 04, slides 19.

questions.question:
A project uses one brace convention, naming scheme, spacing rule, and declaration style. A new 
developer prefers different conventions. What should the developer do?
options: Use personal style in all new files.
Follow the project's existing coding style unless the team decides to change it.
Mix both styles within each method. <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 18 / 65>
Remove formatting entirely.
questions.explanation: Consistency with the existing code base is the lecture's priority. Source: Lecture 04, slides 21.

questions.question:
When code was written by someone outside your project/organization and reused, what does the 
lecture require?
options: Delete the original author information.
Place an attribution/citation near the reused code and identify the source/author as appropriate.
Rename all variables so no citation is needed.
Only cite code if it does not compile.
questions.explanation: The code-citation slide treats source attribution as part of proper documentation. <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 60 / 65> Source: Lecture 04, slides 22.

questions.question: Why might a complex or duplicated expression be assigned to a local variable?
options: To make the program slower
To improve readability, avoid repeated subexpressions, and make intent clearer
To increase coupling
To eliminate all method calls
questions.explanation: The lecture recommends local variables to simplify complex/duplicate expressions and reduce recomputation. Source: Lecture 04, slides 23.

questions.question: Which statement best matches the lecture's general style guidance?
options: Place multiple unrelated statements on each line to save space.
Use the language/project conventions; for this course maintain the common CSCI 2134 style guide.
Ignore existing style when joining a project.
Line length and formatting never affect readability.
questions.explanation: The lecture emphasizes language/project conventions and the course style guide. Source: Lecture 04, slides 24-26.

questions.question: If a team has an established style guide, what is the recommended behavior?
options: Follow it when working on the existing project.
Replace it immediately with your favorite online guide.
Use a different style for every class.
Follow it only for comments, not code.
questions.explanation: The lecture explicitly says to follow the style guidelines of an existing project. Source: Lecture 04, slides 25.

questions.question: Select all that apply. Which are listed costs of bad code?
options: Harder editing/maintenance
More missed deadlines/opportunities
Higher defect risk and loss of trust
Reduced reuse/extensibility/adaptability
Guaranteed lower CPU temperature
questions.explanation: The slide lists maintenance, schedule, cost, defects/reputation, and design-quality consequences. Source: Lecture 04, slides 27.

questions.question: Which statement best summarizes the lecture's key takeaway?
options: Readability depends only on comments.
Readability depends on logical structure, source documentation, and layout/style, and supports broader software quality.
Readable code must always be shorter than unreadable code.
Formatting is more important than functionality in every context.
questions.explanation: This matches the lecture's summary and organizing framework. Source: Lecture 04, slides 28.

questions.question: What is the key economic reason the lecture gives for finding defects early?
options: Early defects are always simpler algorithms.
The earlier a defect is identified or avoided, the cheaper it is to fix.
Late defects cannot be fixed.
Testing becomes free late in development.
questions.explanation: The lecture's central motivation is that defect-fix cost increases the later the defect is detected. Source: Lecture 05, slides 4-5.

questions.question: Which statement about debugging/fixing cost is emphasized in the lecture?
options: Debugging is a negligible part of development time.
Debugging can consume more than half of development time, motivating defect prevention and early detection.
Debugging should occur only after release.
Debugging cost is unrelated to when defects are found. <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 20 / 65>
questions.explanation: The slide cites debugging as taking more than 50% of time and stresses early discovery. Source: Lecture 05, slides 5.

questions.question:
Which activity is categorized primarily as detecting and fixing existing defects rather than avoiding 
them?
options: Set software quality objectives
Use software-engineering guidelines
Perform technical reviews
Allocate time to meet quality objectives
questions.explanation: Technical reviews are listed under detection/fixing; the others are prevention/QA practices. Source: Lecture 05, slides 6.

questions.question: Select all that apply. Which are techniques listed for avoiding software defects?
options: Set software quality objectives
Measure the quality objectives
Use software-engineering guidelines
Use collaborative development

Delete passing tests to reduce work.
questions.explanation: The lecture links minimal code to avoiding overdesign and implementing functionality before it is required. Source: Lecture 07, slides 30.

questions.question: Why can TDD still require refactoring or rework later?

To show that tests should be written only after all methods exist
To replace requirements with random tests

options: Can be difficult to adopt on a code base that already has substantial development
Tests never need maintenance
It prevents all redesign
It makes regression testing impossible
questions.explanation: Legacy adoption, discipline, test maintenance, and possible redesign/refactoring are listed costs. Source: Lecture 07, slides 33.

questions.question: Which statement best summarizes the lecture's final guidance?
options: Unit testing should include boundaries, structured approaches may include basis/path/requirements testing, and TDD integrates tests before implementation and during development.
Only path testing is useful.
Requirements should be ignored once coding begins.
A passing unit-test suite proves the full system is defect-free.

options: Each technique finds different defects at different stages, and no single technique is fully effective.
All techniques are identical, so combining them simplifies training.
Testing alone detects every defect.
Reviews are useful only after release.
questions.explanation: The lecture emphasizes complementary strengths and cites high effectiveness from combining techniques. Source: Lecture 08, slides 4-5.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes testing from debugging?
options: Testing detects defects; debugging diagnoses their causes and corrects them.
Testing fixes defects; debugging only reports them. <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 39 / 65>
Testing and debugging are synonyms.
Debugging must always happen before a defect is detected.

questions.question: Which is a challenge of testing identified in the lecture?
options: Testers must adopt a mindset of trying to break code they believed was correct.
Testing proves there are no defects in all practical systems.
Testing automatically improves code quality without fixes.
Only one testing technique is needed at every stage.
questions.explanation: The lecture lists mindset, no guarantee of absence, no automatic quality improvement, and variety of tests as challenges. Source: Lecture 08, slides 7.

questions.question: What does testing show on its own?
options: Where quality failed by exposing defects
That quality has been improved automatically
That no defects exist anywhere
That the code is maintainable
questions.explanation: The slide says testing does not itself improve quality; it shows when quality failed. Source: Lecture 08, slides 7.

questions.question:
Which testing level focuses on code written by one developer, typically methods/functions/simple 
classes?
options: Unit testing
Integration testing
System testing
Acceptance testing
questions.explanation: Unit testing targets the smallest building blocks and is typically owned by one developer. Source: Lecture 08, slides 8.

questions.question: Which testing level primarily checks code from two or more classes/components coming together?
options: Integration testing
Unit testing
Alpha testing
Usability testing
questions.explanation: Integration testing is defined around combined components and their interfaces. Source: Lecture 08, slides 8.

questions.question: What is regression testing?
options: Re-running previously executed tests to make sure changes have not broken existing behavior
Testing only performance under load
Testing a program for the first time
Inspecting code without executing it
questions.explanation: The lecture defines regression testing as repetition of prior test cases after changes. Source: Lecture 08, slides 8.

questions.question:
Which testing level exercises the software in its final configuration including integration with other 
software/hardware systems?
options: System testing
Unit testing
Code reading
Pair programming
questions.explanation: That is the definition of system testing in the lecture. Source: Lecture 08, slides 8.

questions.question: Which is a nonfunctional testing category listed in the lecture?
options: Security testing <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 40 / 65>
Branch creation testing
Commit testing
Indentation testing
questions.explanation: Security is listed alongside performance, scalability, usability, reliability, recovery, and compatibility. Source: Lecture 08, slides 9.

questions.question: Load testing and stress testing are presented as subtypes/aspects of which broader category?
options: Performance testing
Code review
Unit testing
Documentation testing
questions.explanation: The slide nests load and stress testing under performance testing. Source: Lecture 08, slides 9.

questions.question:

Personal workstation only
Production server
Source repository

options: Production server

questions.explanation: Production is the live-data environment. Source: Lecture 08, slides 10.

questions.question: What is the principle behind unit testing stated in the lecture?
options: Smaller pieces of code are generally easier to test.
Larger systems are always easier to test than methods.
Unit tests require production deployment.
Only customers should write unit tests.
questions.explanation: The lecture explicitly states that smaller code pieces are easier to test. Source: Lecture 08, slides 11.

questions.question: Which mapping is correct?
options: Black box = specification/interface only; white box = specification plus implementation; grey box = specification plus partial implementation knowledge
Black box = full implementation; white box = no implementation; grey box = no specification
All three mean the same thing
Grey box means tests are unfinished
questions.explanation: This is the lecture's three-way distinction. Source: Lecture 08, slides 11-14.

questions.question: Why are black-box test cases often more generic?
options: They are derived from what the interface/specification says, without relying on internal implementation details.
They can only use random inputs.
They are always written after debugging.
They are forbidden from testing boundaries. <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 41 / 65>
questions.explanation: Black-box tests are specification-based, so they do not target internal branches or array sizes unless exposed by the specification. Source: Lecture 08, slides 12.

questions.question:
A developer knows an internal array expands when it reaches a specific size and writes a test exactly 
at that size. What type of test is this most clearly?
options: White-box test
Black-box acceptance test
User-interface test
System deployment test
questions.explanation: The case is based on knowledge of the implementation. Source: Lecture 08, slides 13.

questions.question: What makes a grey-box test different from a white-box test?
options: Grey-box testing uses only partial knowledge/assumptions about the implementation rather than full implementation knowledge.
Grey-box testing never uses the specification.
White-box testing cannot inspect code.
Grey-box testing is always a system test.
questions.explanation: The lecture defines grey box as specification plus partial implementation knowledge. Source: Lecture 08, slides 14.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between unit testing and component testing in this lecture?
options: Scale: component testing covers larger code units and often code produced by multiple developers.
Unit testing uses no code execution.
Component testing cannot use black-box methods.
Unit testing is always performed after system testing.
questions.explanation: The lecture says the core difference is scale and multi-developer familiarity. Source: Lecture 08, slides 15.

questions.question: Which characteristic is central to integration testing?
options: Testing the interactions/interfaces between multiple components that work individually
Testing one isolated method only
Testing only source formatting
Testing only live production data
questions.explanation: Integration testing focuses on combined components and their boundaries/interfaces. Source: Lecture 08, slides 16.

questions.question: Why is black-box testing commonly useful during integration testing?
options: Developers often need to test component interfaces without being equally familiar with all internal implementations.
Integration testing forbids all source-code knowledge.
Black-box tests are the only tests that can run on servers.
Interfaces are irrelevant during integration.
questions.explanation: The lecture notes that cross-team integration often emphasizes externally visible interface behavior. Source: Lecture 08, slides 16.

questions.question: What does the 'testing continuum' slide emphasize?
options: Unit, component, and integration testing differ mainly in scale, and each can mix black-, grey-, and white-box approaches.
Every scale must use a completely different testing philosophy.
White-box testing is limited to system testing.
Unit tests can never become part of higher-level tests.
questions.explanation: The continuum treats the scales similarly while increasing size and team involvement. Source: Lecture 08, slides 17.

questions.explanation: I, II, III, and V are correct; IV is not the definition of regression testing. <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 63 / 65> Source: Lecture 08, slides 18-19.

questions.question: When should testing be performed according to the lecture?
options: As early as possible once there is something to test
Only after all coding is complete
Only after deployment
Only after documentation is finished
questions.explanation: The lecture states 'as early as possible' because early bugs are easier to fix. Source: Lecture 08, slides 20.

questions.question: Which observation is logically necessary before a test can be performed?
options: The test must exist and there must be something implemented to test.
The final system must be deployed.
All requirements must be frozen forever.
A customer must be present.

questions.question:

options: D(n)=b·t·n²

D(n)=b·t

questions.question: Why does testing in small increments reduce total debugging time in the lecture's model?
options: Each defect is found while the relevant code chunk is smaller, so both the number of defects per chunk and the time to isolate/fix each are lower.
Incremental testing makes bugs impossible.
Testing cost is unrelated to code size.
The model assumes no bugs occur in small chunks.
questions.explanation: The lecture contrasts quadratic whole-program debugging with lower cumulative cost across small chunks. Source: Lecture 08, slides 21-24.

questions.question: What does it mean that testing should 'bracket implementation'?
options: Create specification-based tests before coding, run/debug while implementing, and add implementation-aware tests as needed.
Do no testing during coding and run one final test afterward.
Test only before writing any code and never again.
Use only integration tests.
questions.explanation: The slide describes tests before, during, and after implementation. Source: Lecture 08, slides 25.

questions.question: Why does TDD tend to expose difficult cases and requirement ambiguities earlier?
options: Writing tests first forces attention to what the requirement actually means and what cases must be handled before much code exists.
TDD removes all requirements.
TDD delays testing until release.
TDD uses only white-box tests written after implementation.
questions.explanation: The lecture explicitly links pre-code tests to early requirement/design thinking. Source: Lecture 08, slides 26-27.

questions.question: What is scaffolding in testing?
options: Supporting structure created to let tests run parts of the code
A permanent feature of the production user interface
A Git branching strategy
A documentation style guide
questions.explanation: The scaffolding slide defines it as the structure built so tests can invoke/evaluate the target code. Source: Lecture 08, slides 28.

questions.question: When is a shell test script especially appropriate?

Merges the Git branch

A list of source-code comments
A version-control server
A deployment environment with live data
questions.explanation: The lecture describes harnesses as drivers that run/support the target piece of code. Source: Lecture 08, slides 32.

questions.question: What is a stub used for?
options: To simulate a component/dependency that the code under test calls so the target can be tested in isolation
To store the production database permanently
To replace all assertions
To compile the entire project
questions.explanation: Stubs stand in for dependencies and provide predictable responses during isolated testing. Source: Lecture 08, slides 32.

questions.question: Why use a testing framework such as JUnit?
options: It provides standardized harness/support mechanisms so developers can focus on writing tests instead of rebuilding test infrastructure.
It removes the need for expected results.
It prevents tests from being automated.

questions.explanation: Frameworks package common test-harness functionality and test execution. Source: Lecture 08, slides 34-35.

questions.question:

Reformatting source code

Gathering evidence
Testing the fix

questions.question:

I, II, III, IV, and V

questions.question: Why are large numbers of print statements a poor default debugging technique?

Observable only in production with no test

questions.question: Why is a small test case especially useful for debugging?

It guarantees the bug is in the test.

questions.explanation: The slide recommends shrinking the reproducer because it simplifies diagnosis. Source: Lecture 09, slides 10.

Apply random fixes after each run
Replace the entire program immediately
Collect output without changing the hypothesis

questions.question: When gathering data for a debugging hypothesis, what evidence should be considered?

Only the most recent print statement
Only data that supports the first hypothesis
Only compiler warnings
questions.explanation: The lecture advises using all available data and treating negative results as useful evidence. Source: Lecture 09, slides 16.

questions.question: Why can patterns across multiple failing tests be valuable?
options: Failures that share a cause may expose a common point or condition, helping generate a stronger hypothesis.
Patterns prove every failure has a different cause.
They are relevant only to performance testing.
They eliminate the need to reproduce the bug.
questions.explanation: The lecture encourages looking for common points among errors. Source: Lecture 09, slides 16.

questions.question: Which is a reasonable starting place when forming a bug hypothesis?
options: Code that changed recently or has a history of defects
The most stable and well-tested code only
Random code unrelated to the symptom
Only code written by someone else
questions.explanation: Recent changes, historically buggy code, complexity, and common mistakes are suggested starting points. Source: Lecture 09, slides 17.

Sort the source files alphabetically
Prove the bug is in the middle statement
Replace all loops with binary search

Whether the code compiles faster
Whether the branch name is correct <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 48 / 65>
questions.explanation: The search uses symptom presence to choose which half to keep investigating. Source: Lecture 09, slides 18.

Keep testing the same region forever.
Delete all tests.
Fix a nearby symptom even if unrelated.
questions.explanation: The lecture's 'expand the search' slide recommends broadening the suspicious region and retesting hypotheses. Source: Lecture 09, slides 19.

questions.question: Why is a visual debugger generally preferable to extensive print debugging?
options: It can pause execution, inspect variables/data structures, step through code, and watch state without repeatedly editing source for diagnostic prints.
It automatically fixes all defects.
It requires no understanding of program flow.
It only works on programs with no loops.
questions.explanation: Those capabilities are the lecture's argument for debugger tools. Source: Lecture 09, slides 20.

Commit
Stub
Merge

options: Step Over
Step Into
Step Out
Watchpoint
questions.explanation: Step Over runs the next statement while not entering called methods. Source: Lecture 09, slides 21.

questions.question: Which debugger action enters the method being called on the current line?
options: Step Into
Step Over
Continue
Run to cursor
questions.explanation: Step Into descends into the called method. Source: Lecture 09, slides 21.

questions.question: What is a watchpoint?
options: A breakpoint triggered when a watched variable's value changes
A permanent code comment
A test that always passes
A Git tag
questions.explanation: The lecture defines a watchpoint as pausing when a variable changes. Source: Lecture 09, slides 21.

questions.question: Which sequence best matches a typical debugger workflow?
options: Set breakpoint execute to breakpoint inspect/step state continue or adjust breakpoints and repeat → → →
Deploy commit guess print → → →
Delete tests run once fix symptom → → <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 49 / 65>
Start at the end and never inspect variables
questions.explanation: The process slide shows iterative breakpoints, execution, inspection, stepping, and continuation. Source: Lecture 09, slides 22.

questions.question: If you are stuck on a difficult bug, which response is recommended?

Continue the exact same failed approach indefinitely
Remove the failing requirement
Commit a speculative fix without testing
questions.explanation: The lecture gives these as practical ways to reset thinking. Source: Lecture 09, slides 24.

questions.question: How can another developer help when you are stuck?

Guarantee the defect disappears without investigation
Replace the test suite automatically

questions.explanation: The lecture suggests code review/collaboration when individual debugging stalls. Source: Lecture 09, slides 24.

questions.question: What is the lecture's rule for brute-force debugging?

Use it indefinitely until something changes.
Never rerun tests.
Always rewrite the entire program first.
questions.explanation: The lecture says brute force can help but should be time-limited to avoid unproductive effort. Source: Lecture 09, slides 25-26.

questions.question: Which is an example of a brute-force debugging tactic listed in the lecture?
options: Recompile with more warnings and step through execution line by line
Ignore compiler warnings
Remove unit tests
Refuse to reproduce the bug
questions.explanation: The slide lists warnings, line-by-line execution, different environments, backtracking commits, and expanded tests. Source: Lecture 09, slides 25.

questions.question: What is rubber-duck debugging?

Use a debugger shaped like a duck.
Ask a customer to fix the code.
Replace the method with random code.
questions.explanation: The method relies on the cognitive benefit of articulating the problem. Source: Lecture 09, slides 27.

questions.question: Before implementing a bug fix, what should be done?
options: Understand and reproduce the problem, confirm the bug, and preserve/commit the current version
Immediately edit multiple unrelated modules
Delete the failing test
Disable version control
questions.explanation: The pre-fix steps emphasize understanding, reproduction, and preserving the baseline. <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 64 / 65> Source: Lecture 09, slides 28.

questions.question: Which practice best matches the lecture's bug-fix implementation guidance?
options: Fix the root cause with only necessary changes, make one change at a time, verify the fix with tests/regression, and add a test exposing the defect.
Change as much code as possible at once. <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 50 / 65>
Fix only the visible symptom.
Skip testing after the change.
questions.explanation: The implementation slide emphasizes focused root-cause changes and regression protection. Source: Lecture 09, slides 29.

questions.question: Why add a new test after finding and fixing a defect?
options: To capture the defect as a regression case so the same failure is detected if it returns
To increase code size
To replace the original requirement
To avoid looking for similar defects
questions.explanation: The lecture explicitly says to add a unit test that exposes the defect. Source: Lecture 09, slides 29.

questions.question: What should happen after the immediate bug is fixed and verified?
options: Look for similar errors elsewhere in the code base.
Delete the test that exposed the bug.
Assume no related defects can exist.
Reset the repository to before the fix.
questions.explanation: The scientific-debugging process ends by looking for similar errors. Source: Lecture 09, slides 29-30.

questions.question: Which ordering best summarizes the debugging process in the key takeaways?
options: Gather data form hypothesis determine how to test it test/disprove/prove it update understanding → → → → → fix and verify

Commit random change deploy inspect → →
Write documentation assume symptom is root cause →
questions.explanation: The takeaway slide describes iterative hypothesis-driven debugging followed by careful correction. Source: Lecture 09, slides 30.

questions.question: Which set matches the lecture's four broad categories of generic mistakes?
options: Bad code; bad assumptions/poor robustness; logic errors; faulty processes

questions.question: Why does the lecture discuss Therac-25, Ariane 5, and the Boeing 737 MAX?

questions.question: What is 'bad code' in the lecture's classification?

questions.question: What rule does the lecture give for compiler warnings?
options: Code should compile with no warnings.

options: Some control-flow paths may use the variable uninitialized, producing undefined/unintended behavior.
All local variables are automatically zero in every language.
It only affects formatting.
It makes the program too portable.

questions.question: Which statement about warnings best matches the lecture?
options: Warnings may differ by language/compiler, but they usually have a reason and should be investigated rather than ignored.
Warnings are always errors in every language. <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 53 / 65>
Java can never issue warnings.
A deprecated-API warning proves the code will crash.
questions.explanation: The lecture notes language differences while emphasizing that warnings exist for a reason. Source: Lecture 10, slides 11.

questions.question: What is a bad assumption in the lecture's sense?
options: An unstated belief about input, method returns, environment, or resources that the code relies on without ensuring it is valid
A documented precondition that is guaranteed by the specification
A passing unit test
A clear interface contract
questions.explanation: The slide lists assumptions about parameters, returns, inputs, and runtime environment as robustness risks. Source: Lecture 10, slides 12.

questions.question:
A method immediately reads `arr[0]` before checking the array. Which assumptions make the code 
unsafe?
options: That `arr` is non-null and has at least one element
That the array is sorted
That the array uses integers
That the array is local
questions.explanation: The example explicitly assumes non-null and non-empty input. Source: Lecture 10, slides 13.

questions.question:
Code converts a list to an array and immediately compares `arr[0]` and `arr[1]`. What should be 
checked first?
options: That the array contains at least two elements
That the array is sorted
That the list was committed to Git
That all strings use uppercase
questions.explanation: The example's fix is to check the returned array length before indexing. Source: Lecture 10, slides 14.

questions.question:
A program reads a mailbox ID with `Scanner.nextInt()` and then uses it as a list index. Which two 
assumptions should be validated?
options: The user enters an integer and the integer is a valid index/ID
The user enters a floating-point value and the list is empty
The input is already sorted and unique
The program has no tests
questions.explanation: The slide identifies both input-type and valid-range assumptions. Source: Lecture 10, slides 15.

questions.question: What robustness issue is illustrated by attempting to allocate a huge fixed-size 3D array?
options: Assuming sufficient memory/resources will always be available
Using the wrong comparison operator
Comparing strings by reference
Forgetting to sort the array
questions.explanation: The example assumes the program can allocate roughly 4GB and recommends handling resource limits. Source: Lecture 10, slides 16.

questions.question:
Which practices help avoid bad assumptions?
I. Spell out assumptions in the method specification
II. Do not assume more than the specification guarantees
III. Understand boundary conditions before using/implementing a method
IV. Use assertions to enforce assumptions where appropriate
V. Ignore the specification if the code appears to work
options: I, II, III, and IV
I, III, and V
II and V
I, II, III, IV, and V
questions.explanation: I-IV are lecture recommendations; V is directly contrary to them. Source: Lecture 10, slides 17.

questions.question: Which is NOT listed as a common logic error?
options: Off-by-one error
Incorrect comparator
Incorrect loop increment
Forgotten or misordered condition
Correctly validating every boundary condition
questions.explanation: The other four are examples on the logic-errors slide. Source: Lecture 10, slides 18.

questions.question:
A grading rule says 80 and above earns A-, but the code uses `percentage > 80`. What kind of error is 
this?
options: Incorrect comparator / boundary logic error
Version-control failure
Documentation error only
Memory-allocation assumption
questions.explanation: The lecture uses this exact pattern as a comparator/boundary error and fixes it with `>=`. Source: Lecture 10, slides 19.

questions.question: Which testing technique is especially suitable for catching the `> 80` versus `>= 80` mistake?
options: A boundary test at exactly 80
A random test at 95 only
A style review that never runs code
A load test
questions.explanation: The lecture calls this a great boundary-condition example. Source: Lecture 10, slides 19.

questions.question: Why is `str == s` unreliable for checking whether two Java strings contain the same text?
options: It tests whether the references identify the same object rather than comparing string content.
`==` performs lexicographic comparison.
Strings cannot be compared in Java.
`==` checks only the first character.
questions.explanation: The example recommends `str.equals(s)` for content equality. Source: Lecture 10, slides 20.

questions.question: Why can a poorly designed unit test fail to catch the broken `==` string comparison?
options: If the exact same String object is added and searched for, reference equality can accidentally pass even though the method is wrong for equal-but-distinct objects.
JUnit never runs String tests.
Unit tests cannot compare booleans.
The method is actually correct.
questions.explanation: The slide shows a test using the same object that passes despite the defect. Source: Lecture 10, slides 20.

questions.question:
What is the off-by-one error in a loop that compares `arr[i]` with `arr[i+1]` while allowing `i < 
arr.length`?
options: When `i` reaches `arr.length-1`, `arr[i+1]` is out of bounds.
The loop starts at zero.
The array is never modified. <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 55 / 65>
The comparison operator is reversed.
questions.explanation: The fix is to stop at `i < arr.length - 1`. Source: Lecture 10, slides 21.

questions.question: Why must a null check appear before evaluating `n.next == null` in `(n.next == null) || (n == null)`?
options: If `n` is null, accessing `n.next` fails before the second condition can protect it; test `n == null` first.
Java evaluates the right side before the left side.
`||` does not short-circuit.
The two conditions are unrelated.
questions.explanation: Condition order matters because short-circuit evaluation can only protect the dereference if the null check comes first. Source: Lecture 10, slides 22.

questions.question: Which tools/approaches does the lecture recommend for logic errors?
options: Debugger stepping and variable inspection, additional boundary-focused unit tests, assertions, technical reviews, IDE warnings, and coding standards
Only print statements
Only code formatting
No testing because logic errors are unavoidable
questions.explanation: These are the debugging and general approaches listed on the two slides. Source: Lecture 10, slides 23-24.

questions.question: Which is an example of a faulty development process?
options: Infrequent integration
Clear requirements
Consistent version control
Sufficient testing
questions.explanation: Infrequent integration is listed among rush-to-implementation process failures. Source: Lecture 10, slides 25.

questions.question: What root cause does the lecture associate with many faulty-process shortcuts?
options: Time pressure
Too much unit testing
Too many requirements
Excessive documentation quality
questions.explanation: The slide asks this directly and answers with time. Source: Lecture 10, slides 25.

questions.question: Why are poor requirements dangerous?
options: They make it hard to know what to build/test, increase change requests, complicate design, and raise conflict risk.
They guarantee simpler testing.
They eliminate future changes.
They only affect documentation, not implementation.
questions.explanation: These consequences are enumerated on the poor-requirements slide. Source: Lecture 10, slides 26.

questions.question: What pragmatic approach to requirements does the lecture describe?
options: Have most requirements (about 80%) completed before design, expect some evolution, and allocate time to finish the rest.
Freeze 100% of requirements before discussing design under all circumstances.
Start coding with no requirements.
Let each developer invent requirements independently.
questions.explanation: The slide says 100% completeness is impractical and cites an ~80% pre-design practice. Source: Lecture 10, slides 26.

questions.question:
What high-level design information should be established before proceeding too far into 
implementation?
options: Architecture, major components, component interactions, and interfaces/APIs
Every local variable name in every method
Only the color scheme
Only the final test report
questions.explanation: These are the design elements explicitly listed. Source: Lecture 10, slides 27.

questions.question: Which poor implementation practices are called out?
options: Inconsistent guidelines, insufficient version control, and infrequent integration
Frequent commits and integrations
Consistent coding standards
Thorough testing
questions.explanation: Those process problems lead to more work later. Source: Lecture 10, slides 28.

questions.question: What is 'gating' in the context of insufficient testing/documentation?
options: Prevent a developer from moving to the next task until the current work reaches acceptable quality levels
Allow unfinished work to merge faster
Disable tests to meet deadlines
Remove documentation requirements
questions.explanation: The lecture proposes gating as enforcement of quality objectives. Source: Lecture 10, slides 29-30.

questions.question: What quality effects are associated with insufficient documentation?
options: Poor testability, understandability, and maintainability
Higher robustness automatically
Better portability automatically
Fewer future changes
questions.explanation: Those three quality characteristics are explicitly listed as harmed by insufficient documentation. Source: Lecture 10, slides 30.

questions.question:
Which category does the lecture describe as 'hard to avoid' and typically requiring debugging tools to 
rectify?
options: Logic errors
Bad code warnings
Faulty process shortcuts
Missing style guides
questions.explanation: The key-takeaway slide contrasts logic errors with more avoidable bad code/process problems. Source: Lecture 10, slides 31.

questions.question: Which statement best summarizes the lecture's prevention message?
options: Bad code and faulty processes are largely avoidable through good development practices; bad assumptions can be reduced by explicit contracts/validation; logic errors still require systematic testing/debugging.
All errors are equally unavoidable.
Warnings and process discipline do not matter.
Only logic errors deserve testing.
questions.explanation: This reflects the lecture's final classification and recommendations. Source: Lecture 10, slides 31.
